blocks.h: Edge cases checked by running the code
Why is this the same as next permutation?
p: The smallest number bigger than n using the same digits is exactly the next permutation of its digits (see Next Permutation). The only extra step is the 32-bit check.

bullets: Time: O(d), where d is the number of digits.
Space: O(d) for the digit list.

head: Code
What it does

A boolean array is faster than a set for 0…n−1 indexes
Follow `i → nums[i]` until returning to a visited index
In a permutation every walk ends by closing a cycle
The value is the next index

blocks.h: Why is it O(n) and not O(n²)?
p: Every index belongs to exactly one cycle, and `seen` marks the whole cycle on its first visit. Later starts inside an already-walked cycle do no work (the `while` fails immediately and `length` is 0), so each index is walked once overall.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for `seen` (an in-place variant marks `nums` itself for O(1) space).

565.takeaway: A permutation splits into disjoint cycles: walk each cycle once, mark it visited, and track the longest.

p: Capacity 3:

blocks.h: Why keep `size` instead of a tail pointer?
p: With only `head` and `tail`, an empty and a full queue both have `head == tail`, so you need an extra slot or flag. Storing `size` makes both states unambiguous and the tail index is derived: `(head + size) % cap`. Note that after the dequeue the freed slot 0 is reused by the next `enQueue(4)`, which is the 'circular' part.

bullets: Time: O(1) per operation.
Space: O(k).

622.takeaway: Circular buffer: a fixed array, a head index and a size; use modulo arithmetic for wrap-around.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Largest values at the end, smallest (most negative) at the start
Best when the top three are positive (or all numbers are negative)
Two smallest (maybe both negative) times the largest
Two negatives multiply to a positive
Only these two shapes can be the maximum

p: The maximum product of three numbers either has 0 or 2 negative factors (an odd count would make it negative, which is only best if every number is negative, and then the three largest, closest to zero, win). With 2 negatives the best are the two most negative numbers; the third factor is then the biggest number. With no negatives, take the three biggest.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort (O(n) is possible by tracking the top 3 and bottom 2).
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

628.takeaway: Maximum product of three: compare (three largest) with (two smallest × largest) because two negatives make a positive.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Cell → list of cells it sums
A list (not a set) so a cell listed twice counts twice
Remove any formula when `set` overwrites a cell
`None` default avoids an error if there was none
Value = sum of the values of its source cells
Formulas can refer to other formulas

p: 3×C sheet (A–C):

blocks.h: Why compute on read (lazy) instead of storing the sum?
p: If values were stored at `sum` time, every later `set` would have to find and refresh all dependent cells (and dependants of dependants). Evaluating on `get` always sees current inputs, at the price of repeating work: `get(3,'C')` returned 6 after B2 changed with no bookkeeping. The cost depends on the depth/size of the formula graph and can be large for long dependency chains.

blocks.h: Why a list of cells with duplicates?
p: The sum `['A1', 'A1:B2']` includes A1 twice (once alone, once inside the range). The problem counts it twice, so the expansion keeps both entries: here A1 + (A1 + B1 + A2 + B2) = 2 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 4 first, then 6 after B2 = 2.

bullets: Time: `set` O(1); `get`/`sum` cost grows with the total size of the formula tree below the cell (no caching).
Space: O(cells) for the dicts and formula lists.

631.takeaway: Spreadsheet design: store constants and formulas separately, and evaluate formulas recursively on read.

blocks.h: Why process a whole level in an inner loop?
p: `range(n)` with `n = len(q)` consumes exactly the current level; children appended during the loop belong to the next one. Otherwise a single queue would mix levels and the sums couldn't be separated.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(w), the maximum width of the tree.

637.takeaway: Level-order BFS (Breadth-First Search): freeze the queue length per level, sum the values, divide by the count.

Convert the largest sum to an average at the end
Dividing once avoids repeated floating-point work

blocks.h: Why compare sums instead of averages?
p: All windows have the same length k, so the largest sum is the largest average. This keeps the loop in integers and divides once.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

643.takeaway: Fixed-size sliding window: slide by adding the new element and subtracting the old, and compare sums.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Finishing early leaves the most room for later pairs
End of the last pair in the chain
Compare each candidate's start with it
Strictly greater, because `b < c` is required
A pair starting exactly at `end` cannot follow

blocks.h: Why sort by end, not by start?
p: This is the classic interval-scheduling greedy: always pick the pair that ends first among those that fit. Any longer chain can be rearranged to start with it without losing length, since finishing earlier never blocks a later pair. Sorting by start could take a long early pair that blocks several short ones.

bullets: Time: O(n log n).
Space: O(1) besides the sorted copy.

646.takeaway: Interval scheduling greedy: sort by end and take every pair that starts after the last chosen end.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `deque(i for i, c in … if c == 'R')`
Queue of indexes of each party's senators
The next senator of each party
Compare their positions to see who acts first
The earlier senator bans the later one of the other party
Winner goes back to the end of the queue for the next round
Adding n places it after everyone in the next round while keeping the relative order
The other party has been eliminated

p: `'RDD'` gives Dire (and `'RD'` gives Radiant):

head: Step
R queue
D queue
What happens
rows: R0 acts first, bans D1; R re-queued as 3
D2 acts first, bans R3; D re-queued as 5

blocks.h: Why ban the next opponent and why `+ n`?
bullets: Greedy: the best ban is the nearest opposing senator that has not acted yet, because he would otherwise ban one of your party sooner. Comparing the front of each queue does exactly that.
Both queues together always contain each surviving senator once; the winner of the comparison survives and acts again in the next round.
Adding `n` to the survivor's index puts them behind every senator of the current round, preserving round order without an extra data structure.
Time: O(n): each comparison removes one senator, and there are at most n comparisons.
Space: O(n).

649.takeaway: Greedy simulation with two queues of indexes: the earlier senator bans the opponent and rejoins the next round with index + n.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: String of left text, value, right text
A string that uniquely identifies the subtree's shape and values
Without it, different shapes could give the same text
Serialisation → how many times it occurred
Counting starts at 0 for new keys
Add the node once per duplicate group, not on the 3rd, 4th occurrence

p: Tree `[1,2,3,4,null,2,4,null,null,4]`. Serialisations are built bottom-up (post-order); duplicates found: [4, 2] (the subtrees `4` and `2,4`).

blocks.h: Why does the second occurrence trigger the add?
p: Using `== 2` (rather than `>= 2`) reports each duplicated subtree one time even if it appears three or more times, which matches 'one root per group'.

Each node's string includes its whole subtree, so strings can be long (up to O(n) characters on a skewed tree), and building and hashing them costs O(n) per node. Assigning each distinct serialisation a small integer id removes this and gives O(n).

bullets: Time: O(n²) in the worst case.
Space: O(n²) for the stored strings.

652.takeaway: Serialise each subtree bottom-up and count the strings in a dict; add a node when its serialisation is seen the second time.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Candidates for the window's start index
A window of k elements can start at 0 … n−k
Left end `arr[mid]` is farther from x than the element just outside on the right
Then the window starting at mid is worse than one starting at mid+1
Move right / keep mid as a candidate
Binary search for the best start

blocks.h: Why compare the two outer elements, and why is the tie handled by `else`?
p: The best window has its two boundary elements balanced around x. Comparing the distance of `arr[mid]` (about to drop out) with `arr[mid+k]` (about to join) tells which window start is better. On a tie the problem prefers the smaller number, so we keep the left window: `hi = mid`.

bullets: Time: O(log(n − k)) to find the start, plus O(k) for the slice.
Space: O(1) beyond the slice.

658.takeaway: Binary search for the window's start: compare how far the leftmost and the next element to the right are from x.

p: If you overwrote `img` in place, later cells would average already-smoothed neighbours. A new `res` keeps every calculation based on the original image. (An in-place version packs both old and new values into one integer.)

Space: O(m·n) for the result.

661.takeaway: Average each 3×3 neighbourhood with clipped bounds; write to a new grid so every cell uses original values.

p: `'abca'` (already without consecutive repeats): `dp[i][j]` for interval i..j (blank cells are below the diagonal):

`dp[0][3] = 3`: print `a` over the whole span first (1 turn), then `b` and `c` inside: `abca` needs 3 turns instead of 4 because the two `a`s share one turn. For `'aaabaaa'` the groups collapse to `aba` and the answer is 2.

bullets: Time: O(n³): n² intervals, each trying up to n split points.
Space: O(n²).

664.takeaway: Interval DP: the first character can share a turn with any later equal character, splitting the interval around it.

How many such longest subsequences end at i

Another chain of the same best length

p: `[1,3,5,4,7]`; the longest length is 4:

Two chains of length 3 end before 7: `1,3,5` (ends at 5) and `1,3,4` (ends at 4). Each extends by 7, so `count[4] = count[2] + count[3] = 1 + 1 = 2`. These are the two answers `1,3,5,7` and `1,3,4,7`.

bullets: Time: O(n²).
Space: O(n).

673.takeaway: LIS (Longest Increasing Subsequence) DP carrying a second array: the number of ways to reach each best length.

`rest = [nums[k] … if k != i and k != j]`
The numbers not used in this step
Possible results of combining a and b

p: `[4,1,8,7]` is True (the code finds a way; this is the first successful chain of combinations it reached, step by step):
`[1,2,1,2]` returns False: every sequence of combinations is tried and none ends within 1e-6 of 24.

With 4 cards there are 12 ordered pairs × 4 operations at the first level, 6 × 4 at the second, 2 × 4 at the last: a few thousand states at most. Parentheses are implicit: combining two numbers into a new number at each step covers every bracket arrangement.

bullets: Time: O(1): a fixed number of cards gives a bounded search (about 12·4 · 6·4 · 2·4 combinations).
Space: O(1).

679.takeaway: Search by combining any two numbers with each operation until one remains; compare with 24 using a tolerance because of float division.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The 8 knight moves as (row, column) offsets
Loop over offsets instead of eight copies of the code
Probability the knight is on (r, c) after the moves made so far
Probability mass spreads move by move
A fresh grid for the next move
All cells of a move must be computed from the previous move's grid
Each of the 8 moves has probability 1/8
Mass sent to every target square, including off-board ones (those are lost)
Total probability remaining on the board

p: `n = 3`, `k = 2`, start (0,0); each grid shows probabilities per cell (rows separated by `/`). The final total is 0.0625:

From the corner (0,0) only two of the eight moves stay on the 3×3 board, to (1,2) and (2,1), so after one move the knight is on the board with probability 2/8 = 0.25. Each of those two squares again has exactly two moves that stay on the board, so the remaining probability is 0.25 · 2/8 = 0.0625.

bullets: Time: O(k·n²·8).
Space: O(n²).

688.takeaway: Probability DP: spread each cell's probability to its on-board knight targets one move at a time; whatever leaves the board is dropped.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Uses the grid as the visited marker
Cell position relative to the island's first (top-left-most) cell
Translation-invariant signature: moving the island doesn't change it
Lists can't go in a set; tuples can
Every DFS (Depth-First Search) visits neighbours in the same order
Equal shapes then produce identical sequences of offsets

p: Grid `11011 / 10000 / 00001 / 11011`: each row is one island found, its offsets in visit order, and whether the shape is new. Distinct shapes: 3.

blocks.h: Why relative offsets instead of absolute coordinates?
p: Two islands count as the same shape if one can be translated onto the other. Absolute coordinates would make every island unique; subtracting the starting cell turns each island into a position-independent signature. No rotation or reflection is allowed, so no extra normalisation is needed.

bullets: Time: O(m·n).
Space: O(m·n) for shapes and recursion.

694.takeaway: Canonical shape signature: record each island's cells relative to its start in a fixed DFS (Depth-First Search) order and count distinct signatures.

Occurrence count (a `Counter` returns 0 for missing keys)
Length of the span from x's first to current occurrence
Shortest subarray containing all copies of x so far
`cnt[x] > deg or (cnt[x] == deg and length < best)`
Higher degree wins; on a tie the shorter span wins

blocks.h: Why does the span from the first occurrence work?
p: A subarray with the same degree must contain every copy of some most frequent value, so its minimum length is (last − first + 1) for that value. Computing the span at each occurrence and keeping the smallest among values with the top count finds it in one pass.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(n).

697.takeaway: Track first index and count per value: the answer is the shortest first-to-last span among the most frequent values.
